evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on connectivity patterns.

claim: Previous work on the neural basis of intelligence has focused on coarse-grained features of brain anatomy and function.
source: Previous work on the neural basis of intelligence, however, has focused on coarse-grained features of brain anatomy and function because cortical topographies are highly idiosyncratic at a finer scale, obscuring individual differences in fine-grained connectivity patterns.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Cortical topographies are highly idiosyncratic at a finer scale.
source: Previous work on the neural basis of intelligence, however, has focused on coarse-grained features of brain anatomy and function because cortical topographies are highly idiosyncratic at a finer scale, obscuring individual differences in fine-grained connectivity patterns.

claim: Idiosyncratic cortical topographies obscure individual differences in fine-grained connectivity patterns.

claim: Hyperalignment can resolve topographic idiosyncrasies in cortical connectivity patterns.
source: We used a computational algorithm, hyperalignment, to resolve these topographic idiosyncrasies and found that predictions of general intelligence based on fine-grained (vertex-by-vertex) connectivity patterns were markedly stronger than predictions based on coarse-grained (region-by-region) patterns.
evidence: The study demonstrates this through experimental application of hyperalignment.

claim: Predictions of general intelligence based on fine-grained connectivity patterns are markedly stronger than predictions based on coarse-grained patterns.
source: We used a computational algorithm, hyperalignment, to resolve these topographic idiosyncrasies and found that predictions of general intelligence based on fine-grained (vertex-by-vertex) connectivity patterns were markedly stronger than predictions based on coarse-grained (region-by-region) patterns.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intelligence is best predicted by fine-grained connectivity in the default cortical system.
source: Intelligence was best predicted by fine-grained connectivity in the default and frontoparietal cortical systems, both of which are associated with self-generated thought.
evidence: This finding is supported by the experimental results shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Intelligence is best predicted by fine-grained connectivity in the frontoparietal cortical system.

claim: Regional hyperaligned fine-grained task connectivity profiles accounted for 27.3% of variance in general intelligence on average across all cortical regions.

claim: Prediction models based on coarse-grained task fMRI connectivity accounted on average for only 14.9% of variance in general intelligence.
source: By contrast, prediction models based on coarse-grained task fMRI connectivity (Figure 3B) accounted on average for only 14.9% of variance (min: 3.3%; max: 26.5%), which is only 54.2% (95% CI: [48.7%, 58.8%]) of VAF by hyperaligned fine-grained connectivity overall.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data.

claim: VAF by hyperaligned fine-grained task connectivity was higher than VAF by coarse-grained connectivity in all 360 ROIs.

claim: The 30 most predictive regions (33.8–38.9% VAF) were in bilateral inferior parietal cortex (15 regions), bilateral medial and superior prefrontal cortex (11 regions), bilateral medial parietal (2 regions), and bilateral posterior lateral temporal cortex (2 regions).
source: The 30 most predictive regions (Figure 3D, E; 33.8–38.9% VAF) were in bilateral inferior parietal cortex (15 regions), bilateral medial and superior prefrontal cortex (11 regions), bilateral medial parietal (2 regions), and bilateral posterior lateral temporal cortex (2 regions).

claim: The cortices in the 30 most predictive regions were predominantly part of the default mode and frontoparietal systems (38.9% and 34.5% of cortical vertices, respectively).
source: The cortices in these regions were predominantly part of the default mode and frontoparietal systems (38.9% and 34.5% of cortical vertices, respectively) with small portions in the ventral and dorsal attention systems (11.3% and 10.6%, respectively; Figure 3D, E; Yeo et al., 2011).
evidence: This finding is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Models based on hyperaligned fine-grained resting fMRI connectivity accounted on average for 19.8% of variance in general intelligence.
source: Models based on hyperaligned fine-grained resting fMRI connectivity accounted on average for 19.8% of variance (Figure 4A; min: 4.7%; max: 31.2%), whereas models based on coarse-grained connectivity accounted on average for 8.1% of variance (Figure 4B; min: −1.2%; max: 17.4%), which is only 40.5% [CI: 34.2%, 45.8%] of VAF by hyperaligned fine-grained resting connectivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Models based on coarse-grained resting fMRI connectivity accounted on average for 8.1% of variance in general intelligence.

claim: Hyperaligned fine-grained resting fMRI connectivity accounted for more variance than coarse-grained resting fMRI connectivity in all 360 ROIs.

claim: Task fMRI connectivity is significantly more predictive of general intelligence than resting fMRI connectivity for both hyperaligned fine-grained data and coarse-grained data.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Greene et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2020), task fMRI connectivity was significantly more predictive of general intelligence than was resting fMRI connectivity for both hyperaligned fine-grained data (difference = 7.6% VAF; 95% CI: [5.3%, 9.9%]) and coarse-grained data (difference = 6.8% VAF; 95% CI: [5.0%, 8.6%]).

claim: Models based on MSM-aligned fine-grained task connectivity accounted for, on average across ROIs, 17.6% of variance in general intelligence.
source: Models based on MSM-aligned fine-grained task connectivity and resting connectivity accounted for, on average across ROIs, 17.6% (min: 5.1%; max: 28.7%) and 11.1% (min: 0.8%; max: 22.5%), respectively, of variance in general intelligence, which was 64.3% (95% CI: [59.9%, 68.3%]) and 56.0% (95% CI: [49.7%, 61.7%]) of that accounted for by models using hyperaligned data (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Models based on MSM-aligned fine-grained resting connectivity accounted for, on average across ROIs, 11.1% of variance in general intelligence.
source: Models based on MSM-aligned fine-grained task connectivity and resting connectivity accounted for, on average across ROIs, 17.6% (min: 5.1%; max: 28.7%) and 11.1% (min: 0.8%; max: 22.5%), respectively, of variance in general intelligence, which was 64.3% (95% CI: [59.9%, 68.3%]) and 56.0% (95% CI: [49.7%, 61.7%]) of that accounted for by models using hyperaligned data (Figure 5).

claim: Hyperalignment factors out idiosyncrasies in functional topography to reveal how individuals differ in information encoded in fine-grained cortical functional architecture.

claim: Individual differences in fine-grained patterns of functional connectivity are a markedly better predictor of general intelligence than are coarse-grained patterns.

evidence: This describes the method used in the study, supported by citations.

claim: For each of the 59,412 cortical vertices, the connectivity profile is computed as the correlations between its own time series and the 360 regional average time series.

claim: Hyperalignment derives a transformation matrix for each individual using connectivity profiles, which remixes each individual's vertices into a common set of model dimensions through an improper rotation of a high-dimensional space.
source: In each brain region, we derived a transformation matrix for each individual using these connectivity profiles, which remixes each individual's vertices into a common set of model dimensions through an improper rotation of a high-dimensional space.
evidence: This describes the method used in the study.

claim: Each model dimension has similar functional properties across individuals instead of the same anatomical position.
source: Each model dimension has similar functional properties across individuals instead of the same anatomical position, and these model dimensions together constitute a common model space.

claim: The information content in each individual's data is perfectly preserved during the hyperalignment rotation.
source: The information content in each individual's data—the configuration of connectivity vectors in the high-dimensional feature space—is perfectly preserved during the rotation, whereas how and where this information is encoded in idiosyncratic topographies is factored out into the transformation matrix.
evidence: This describes a property of the hyperalignment method.

claim: Hyperalignment was performed for each brain region separately.
source: In this study, hyperalignment was performed for each brain region separately (i.e., in a similar manner to Haxby et al., 2011 rather than Guntupalli et al., 2016), and the transformation was constrained to be an improper rotation (i.e., rotation that allows reflection) with no scaling.
evidence: This describes the method used in the study.

claim: The hyperalignment transformation was constrained to be an improper rotation with no scaling.
source: In this study, hyperalignment was performed for each brain region separately (i.e., in a similar manner to Haxby et al., 2011 rather than Guntupalli et al., 2016), and the transformation was constrained to be an improper rotation (i.e., rotation that allows reflection) with no scaling.
evidence: This describes the method used in the study.

claim: For each of 360 cortical regions, a fine-grained connectivity matrix was computed for each participant, which comprises pairwise interactions between all vertices in the region and all vertices of the cerebral cortex.
source: For each of 360 cortical regions, we computed a fine-grained connectivity matrix for each participant (Figure 1, top row), which comprises pairwise interactions between all vertices in the region (165 vertices on average) and all vertices of the cerebral cortex (59,412 vertices).
evidence: This describes the method used in the study, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The full fine-grained connectivity profile comprises millions of connectivity strengths (9.8 million on average across all regions).
source: We vectorized this connectivity matrix to form a long vector comprising millions of connectivity strengths (9.8 million on average across all regions), which we refer to as the participant's full fine-grained connectivity profile of the region.
evidence: This describes the method used in the study.

claim: The fine-grained connectivity profile contains information encoded in fine-grained connectivity patterns up to the same resolution as the input fMRI data (2 mm for this dataset).
source: This fine-grained connectivity profile depicts in detail the region's information exchange with the rest of the cortex, and it contains information encoded in fine-grained connectivity patterns up to the same resolution as the input fMRI data (2 mm for this dataset).
evidence: This describes a property of the connectivity profile.

claim: The coarse-grained connectivity profile for a given region is a vector comprising 360 elements.
source: The coarse-grained connectivity profile for a given region is a vector comprising 360 elements, where each element is the average connectivity strength between all cortical vertices in this region and all vertices in another region (Figure 1, middle row).
evidence: This describes the method used in the study, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: A residual fine-grained connectivity profile comprises pattern residuals obtained by subtracting the mean connectivity with each region from each element of the vertex-by-vertex connectivity pattern with the region.
source: A residual fine-grained connectivity profile comprises pattern residuals obtained by subtracting the mean connectivity with each region (an element of the coarse-grained connectivity profile) from each element of the vertex-by-vertex connectivity pattern with the region (part of the full fine-grained connectivity profile).
evidence: This describes the method used in the study.

claim: A regression model using coarse-grained connectivity profile as the independent variable and fine-grained connectivity profile as the dependent variable will always have a slope of 1.
source: Because a coarse-grained connectivity profile comprises region-by-region averages of the corresponding fine-grained connectivity profile, a regression model using coarse-grained connectivity profile (expanded to the same size as the fine-grained connectivity profile) as the independent variable and fine-grained connectivity profile as the dependent variable will always have a slope of 1.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the relationship between the two types of profiles.

claim: The difference between the full fine-grained connectivity profile and the coarse-grained connectivity profile is the residual of the regression model.
source: Therefore, the difference between the two profiles is also the residual of the regression model.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the relationship between the two types of profiles.

claim: A residual fine-grained connectivity profile contains only fine-scale information instead of combined fine- and coarse-scale information.
source: Similar to a full fine-grained connectivity profile, a residual fine-grained connectivity profile comprises millions of elements, and the only difference is that these elements are connectivity residuals instead of connectivities. In other words, a residual fine-grained connectivity profile contains only fine-scale information instead of combined fine- and coarse-scale information.
evidence: This describes a property of the residual connectivity profile.
